quotes.quote: Large multimodal models (LMMs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for long video understanding (LVU), prompting the development of standardized LVU benchmarks to evaluate their performance.
most existing benchmarks rely heavily on multiple-choice questions (MCQs), whose evaluation results are inflated due to the possibility of guessing the correct answer
a significant portion of questions in these benchmarks have strong priors to allow models to answer directly without even reading the input video
video LMMs show drastic performance (>25%) drops on open-ended questions compared with MCQs
higher MCQ scores do not lead to higher open-ended scores on VideoEval-Pro
compared to other MCQ benchmarks, VideoEval-Pro benefits more from increasing the number of input frames
we present V IDEO E VAL -P RO, a more robust and realistic long video understanding benchmark containing open-ended, short-answer QA problems
Our final benchmark contains a total of 1,289 short-answer questions based on 465 videos, with an average duration of 38 minutes.
Current LMMs achieve only ∼10% accuracy on V IDEO E VAL -P RO with a single input frame
LMMs perform better at questions about local video segments and struggle more with those requiring holistic video understanding

we source the questions from four existing long video understanding MCQ benchmarks: Video-MME [2], MLVU [19], LVBench [1] and LongVideoBench [20], and reformat these questions into free-form questions
Our initial seed question set contains a total of 5,562 questions, which are all in MCQ format with 4-6 options.
the correct MCQ option becomes the reference answer, while the distractors are discarded
the models receive only the question itself, forcing them to generate an answer based on the input video rather than exploiting hints from different options
we filter out all samples associated with videos shorter than 10 minutes
we remove questions for which the average word count of answer options in the original MCQ format exceeds five words
We prompt Gemini-2.0-Flash with the question (excluding the answer choices) and ask it to determine whether the question can be answered solely based on the video content.
we randomly sample a single frame from each input video and prompt Gemini-2.0-Flash to generate an answer to the corresponding MCQ and open-ended question using only that frame
Questions for which Gemini-2.0-Flash produces a correct response on both MCQ and open-ended formats are excluded from the benchmark.
Our final dataset comprises 1,289 question-answer pairs in free-form QA, each grounded in a long video with a duration greater than 10 minutes.
includes a total of 465 videos, with an average length of 38.25 minutes
204 videos are between 10 and 30 minutes and 261 videos exceed 30 minutes
371 are associated with videos in the 10–30 minute range, while 918 are based on videos longer than 30 minutes
The average length of an answer is 2.1 words.
LVBench accounts for the largest portion, contributing 714 questions (55%) due to its long and information-rich video sources
MLVU contributes 267 questions (21%), with many QAs excluded because of the relatively short video lengths
Video-MME adds 272 questions (21%)
LongVideoBench, which is smaller in scale and subject to strict selection criteria, contributes 36 questions (3%)
we propose a unified and generalizable task taxonomy to categorize our benchmark questions into four main types and 15 subtypes
The majority of questions (59%) fall under Local Perception
Holistic Reasoning accounts for 21% of the questions, while Local Reasoning and Holistic Perception represent 11% and 10%
Local Perception (LP): LP focuses on identifying and retrieving visual elements or actions from a short video clip in a long video.
Local Reasoning (LR): LR focuses on reasoning within short temporal windows, such as inferring causality, temporal order, or changes that happen over a local sequence of events.
In V IDEO E VAL -P RO, HP is comprised of Visual Counting problems.
Holistic Reasoning (HR): HR requires abstract or high-level understanding of long videos across events or scenes, often involving narrative or intent understanding.
we uniformly sample a fixed number of frames from the corresponding video
we adopt the evaluation criteria introduced in SimpleQA [40] and Video-SimpleQA [41]
We follow the LLM-as-a-Judge [42, 43] paradigm and employ GPT-4o-0806 as our evaluation model to assess the accuracy of generated short answers.
we report the overall correct rate as the proportion of responses labelled "Correct" across the entire dataset
Note that we do not report the F-score (harmonic mean of overall correct and correct given attempted) adopted in SimpleQA and Video-SimpleQA
Correct: The predicted answer comprehensively includes all essential information present in the reference answer and contains no contradictory content.
Not Attempted: The predicted answer omits critical elements of the reference answer but does not contradict it, or the model refuses to answer the question.
We consider a total of 21 proprietary and open-source LMMs and conduct evaluations on our V IDEO E VAL -P RO.
we evaluate each one with inputs of 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512 frames and report its highest score
For all models and the LLM judge, we use greedy decoding (set temperature to 0) to ensure deterministic outputs.
we rerun the evaluation and provide the original answer options to each model
All models are prompted to output only the selected choice, and accuracy is computed via exact string matching.
GPT-4.1 [46] delivers the strongest performance among proprietary models, while Qwen2.5-VL [23] leads the open-source models.
the scores obtained from MCQ and open-ended questions are not necessarily correlated
These findings suggest that MCQ-based accuracy may overestimate model performance and fail to capture the true capacity of models to understand long videos.
we observe that most models perform better on local tasks, suggesting that holistic tasks are generally more challenging
models tend to perform considerably better on perception tasks than on reasoning tasks in the open-ended setting
their performances on V IDEO E VAL -P RO are lagging behind GPT-4o/Gemini-1.5-Pro by 13%
both proprietary and open-source models achieve around 45% accuracy under this setting, with Gemini-1.5-Pro surpassing 50% accuracy
all models achieve only around 10% accuracy on our V IDEO E VAL -P RO when provided with a single input frame
all models achieve their highest accuracy on Video-MME with 256 input frames, but performance begins to plateau or drop when the input is extended to 512 frames
the five tested models exhibit a consistent improvement in accuracy on V IDEO E VAL -P RO as the number of input frames increases
LLM judges may exhibit biases from their training data, which may affect their consistency and fairness during evaluation
we apply a specific version of GPT-4o (GPT-4o-0806) to ensure the fairness of the judgement, which could become outdated and eventually inaccessible after the model provider stops its service
We ran all experiments for open-source models on NVIDIA A800 GPUs.
A 7B-scale model takes approximately 8-10 hours to finish evaluation on a single A800 80G GPU based on 256 frame inputs and 15-20 hours based on 512 frames.
approximately 25K input tokens per query for 256 input frames
Our LLM judge consumes another 10K input tokens per judgement request.
the best-performing model GPT-4.1 achieving 40.8% accuracy
performance on V IDEO E VAL -P RO consistently improves as more frames are provided
reformulates MCQ problems into open-ended questions, preventing models from exploiting shortcuts inherent in the options
VideoEval-Pro includes a total of 465 videos, with an average length of 38.25 minutes.
As different candidate models are trained using different numbers of frames, we evaluate each one with inputs of 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512 frames and report its highest score.

VideoEval-Pro is a robust and realistic long video understanding benchmark containing open-ended, short-answer QA problems.
The dataset is constructed by reformatting questions from four existing long video understanding MCQ benchmarks: Video-MME, MLVU, LVBench, and LongVideoBench into free-form questions.
